beats.narration_text: A chatbot looks like it answers questions. Underneath, it runs one prediction in a loop: given this text, what comes next? The machine inside that prediction is a transformer.

show.event: context title and three cards: Given / Predict / Repeat
writer types 'A chatbot answers questions.'
'answers' and 'questions' turn terracotta, deleted, retyped as 'predicts' and 'text'
final: 'A chatbot predicts text.'

beats.narration_text: Earlier models, called RNNs, read text one word at a time, each step waiting on the last. The transformer, from the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, reads the whole context at once. That made training on hundreds of billions of tokens practical. Generating a reply is still one token at a time.

show.event: lane 'RNN: one word at a time': tiles 'She swung the cricket bat hard' light left to right
lane 'transformer: whole context at once': all tiles light together
label: made training on hundreds of billions of tokens practical
lane 'generating a reply': new tokens append one at a time
citation Vaswani et al., 2017

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole architecture at a glance. Input tokens become vectors plus position, pass through a stack of transformer blocks, and come out as scores, which softmax turns into probabilities. Each block has two parts: attention, then a feed-forward layer, and each adds its result to the vector instead of replacing it, a residual connection. Attention is multi-head: several run side by side, each tracking a different kind of relationship. GPT-3 has ninety-six heads in each of its ninety-six layers.

show.event: top row: input tokens → vectors + position → stack of transformer blocks → output scores → softmax → probabilities
zoom: one block = attention, then feed-forward
residual stream: each part's result is added (+) to the vector, not replacing it
attention splits into several heads side by side
label: GPT-3, 96 heads in each of 96 layers

beats.narration_text: The original 2017 transformer had an encoder and a decoder, because it was built for translation. The encoder reads the source sentence. The decoder writes the translation with two attentions: masked self-attention over what it has written, and cross-attention that reads the encoder's output.

show.event: encoder stack reads 'source sentence'; decoder stack writes 'translation'
inside the decoder: 'masked self-attention' (over what it has written) and 'cross-attention' with an arrow from the encoder
label: built for translation

beats.narration_text: Chat models like GPT keep only the decoder and its masked self-attention, with no encoder and no cross-attention. Now let's walk through it, piece by piece.

show.event: GPT: a single decoder stack with 'masked self-attention'
encoder and cross-attention shown struck out: not used
'predicts the next token'; line: now, piece by piece

beats.narration_text: Each token becomes a vector, a list of numbers, because training only works on continuous values. GPT-3 uses twelve thousand two hundred eighty-eight per token. Position is added too, or Alice paid Bob and Bob paid Alice would look identical.

show.event: one-step pipeline diagram draws; 'tokens' and 'vectors' light
a token turns into a tall strip of number cells
label: 12,288 numbers per token (GPT-3)
'Alice paid Bob' and 'Bob paid Alice' as word sets: '=' without position
position tags 1 2 3 added: '≠'

beats.narration_text: Attention lets vectors revise each other by context: bat after cricket ends up in a different place than bat after fruit.

show.event: pipeline; 'attention' lights
one 'bat' arrow; 'cricket' pulls a copy one way, 'fruit' pulls another copy the other way
two bat arrows end in different places; label 'schematic'

beats.narration_text: Each token's query is matched against the keys. Softmax turns those scores into weights, and each token gathers from the tokens it weights most, only earlier ones.

show.event: query and key tags on each token
query × key → scores → softmax → weights, left to right
weighted arrows gather into the current token, thick for high weight
triangle grid: each token sees only earlier tokens; later cells blocked

beats.narration_text: Feed-forward layers then work on each token separately, adding patterns stored in training, and they hold most of the parameters. The pair repeats: ninety-six layers in GPT-3.

show.event: pipeline; 'feed-forward' lights
one feed-forward box per token, no arrows between tokens
label: holds most of the parameters
attention + feed-forward block stacks: layer 1, 2, 3 … 96 (GPT-3)

beats.narration_text: After the last layer, the vector at the final position, shaped by everything before it, becomes one score, a logit, for every token in the vocabulary, about fifty thousand of them. Softmax turns them into probabilities. So softmax appears twice: inside attention, and here at the output.

show.event: pipeline; 'scores' and 'softmax' light
final-position vector fans into a long row of score bars: '≈ 50,000 logits'
softmax turns them into probabilities
both softmax spots marked in the diagram, inside attention and at the output: 'softmax × 2'

beats.narration_text: That last step is small enough to build by hand. Take three scores: one, two, three. Exponentiate each, then divide by the total. Out come zero point zero nine, zero point two four, and zero point six seven.

show.event: code card: softmax by hand
recorded output [0.09, 0.24, 0.67]

props.title: evidence/softmax_by_hand.py — recorded run
props.code:
import math

scores = [1, 2, 3]
weights = [math.exp(s) for s in scores]   # exponentiate each
total = sum(weights)
probs = [w / total for w in weights]      # divide by the total

print([round(p, 2) for p in probs])
# recorded output:
# [0.09, 0.24, 0.67]

beats.narration_text: Here's the catch. Researchers designed the operations, not the behavior. Nobody wrote code for grammar or translation. Those abilities emerged from fitting billions of parameters, and nobody can read off why a particular prediction was made.

show.event: left 'designed': vectors, attention, feed-forward, softmax
right 'not written': grammar, translation, each struck 'no code'
a dense field of cells labelled 'billions of fitted parameters'
line: nobody can read off why a prediction was made

beats.narration_text: Asking the model doesn't settle it, because its explanation is just more predicted text. In Anthropic's 2025 paper, On the Biology of a Large Language Model, researchers traced a model solving a two-digit addition problem through parallel internal pathways. Asked how, it described the carry-the-one method from school.

show.event: 'its explanation = more predicted text'
left 'traced inside': a two-digit addition (digit boxes) splits into parallel pathways that merge into the answer (schematic)
right 'what the model said': carry-the-one column addition with digit boxes
citation: Anthropic, 2025

beats.narration_text: The verdict. One prediction, in a loop. Tokens become vectors, attention and feed-forward repeat layer after layer, ninety-six times in GPT-3, and softmax turns the final vector into probabilities. The operations were designed. The behavior emerged from fitting. The model decided X because Y is a story, not a measurement.
